Confidence intervals on the per-slice scores

Source: R/confidence.R
score_confidence.Rd

A per-slice score is a proportion estimated from a handful of cases, and a proportion from a handful of cases is noise with a decimal point. A slice of three cases that all passed scores 1.0, and a slice of three hundred that all passed also scores 1.0; [readiness()] treats the two identically and [suite_audit()] can only warn that the first is "too thin" without saying how thin. This puts a number on it.

Usage

score_confidence(run, thresholds = NULL, rep = 1L, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

run

An `r4agent_run`.

thresholds

Optional `r4agent_thresholds`. When given, each slice's threshold and the two clearance decisions are attached.

rep

Which repeat to score.

conf_level

Confidence level, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. Defaults to 0.95.

Value

A data frame of class `r4agent_confidence`, one row per slice plus a TOTAL row, with columns `slice`, `cases`, `score`, `lower` and `upper`, and, when `thresholds` are supplied, `threshold`, `clears_point` and `clears_lower` (the last two are `NA` on the TOTAL row, which has no threshold of its own).

Details

For each slice it returns the score from [score_slices()] with a lower and an upper bound at `conf_level`, computed as a Wilson score interval. A "warn" counts as half, exactly as everywhere else in the package, so the score is the mean of per-case scores of 0, 0.5 or 1 and the interval is around that mean. For a slice that contains warns the interval is an approximation (an interval on an effective pass proportion), which is the honest state of affairs for the bounded mean of a few discrete values.

The Wilson interval is used rather than the textbook normal approximation because the normal one is useless at the edges, and the edges are where a benchmark lives: a slice that passed every case has a point estimate of 1, where the normal interval has zero width and claims certainty from three observations. Wilson does not, and it is a closed form that needs no resampling and no seed, so the bounds are reproducible from the run alone.

When `thresholds` are supplied the slice's threshold is attached together with two decisions: `clears_point`, whether the point score meets it (what [readiness()] uses), and `clears_lower`, whether even the lower bound meets it. A slice that clears on the point estimate but not on the lower bound has not been shown to clear; it simply has too few cases to tell. That distinction is the whole reason this function exists. It changes no score and no verdict: [readiness()] is unchanged and this is an opt-in second look.

See also

[score_slices()], [readiness()], [suite_audit()]

Examples

suite <- agent_suite(list(
  agent_case("a1", "x", "1", grader = "contains", slice = "small"),
  agent_case("a2", "x", "1", grader = "contains", slice = "small"),
  agent_case("a3", "x", "1", grader = "contains", slice = "small")
))
run <- run_benchmark(suite, function(i) "1", quiet = TRUE)
# Three for three is a perfect point score and a wide interval.
score_confidence(run)
#> 
#> ── Per-slice score with 95% confidence interval ────────────────────────────────
#> small 1.0000 [0.4385, 1.0000] (n = 3)
#> TOTAL 1.0000 [0.4385, 1.0000] (n = 3)

# With thresholds, the point score clears 0.9 but the lower bound does not:
# three cases are not enough to claim the slice is ready.
score_confidence(run, agent_thresholds(default = 0.9))
#> 
#> ── Per-slice score with 95% confidence interval ────────────────────────────────
#> [~] small 1.0000 [0.4385, 1.0000] vs 0.9 (n = 3)
#> TOTAL 1.0000 [0.4385, 1.0000] (n = 3)
#> 
#> [v] lower bound clears [~] only the point estimate clears [x] neither
